Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Missouri credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Missouri Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Missouri:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Missouri Federal Bankruptcy Data

When garnishment cannot be stopped administratively, bankruptcy's automatic stay halts it immediately. These FJC numbers show how Missouri debtors use the bankruptcy remedy.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 45,771 consumer bankruptcy cases from Missouri's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 722,13299.0%0.8%

Chapter 1323,63955.1%44.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Can You Recover Missouri Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Missouri Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Head-of-family can cut garnishment by 60% (RSMo 525.030).

If you qualify, file the Missouri exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Missouri

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Missouri creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Missouri exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Missouri bank account levy for the full playbook.

Missouri Garnishment Duration and Release

In Missouri, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Missouri judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Missouri judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Missouri law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

## Wage Garnishment in Montana [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/montana.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Montana [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Montana residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Montana

Montana follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Montana ruleFollows federal CCPA.

Additional protectionNo additional state limit.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which Montana Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In Montana, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Montana credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Montana Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Montana:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Can You Recover Montana Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Montana Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

No additional state limit.

If you qualify, file the Montana exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Montana

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Montana creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Montana exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Montana bank account levy for the full playbook.

Montana Garnishment Duration and Release

In Montana, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Montana judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Montana judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Montana law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

Wage Garnishment in Nebraska [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Nebraska residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Nebraska

Nebraska has a tiered wage-garnishment system that can dramatically reduce the amount taken for heads of households or lower earners. Getting the right classification matters.

LimitRule

Maximum %25% or 15%

Nebraska rule25% max; 15% for heads of households; 85% of disposable exempt.

Additional protectionStrong head-of-household protection.

Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/new-jersey.html

Wage Garnishment in New Jersey [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Jersey residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in New Jersey

New Jersey has a tiered wage-garnishment system that can dramatically reduce the amount taken for heads of households or lower earners. Getting the right classification matters.

LimitRule

Maximum %10% or 25%

New Jersey rule10% max for earners below threshold; 25% otherwise.

Additional protectionTwo-tier protection (N.J.S.A. 2A:17-56).

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which New Jersey Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In New Jersey, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your New Jersey credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop New Jersey Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in New Jersey:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

When garnishment cannot be stopped administratively, bankruptcy's automatic stay halts it immediately. These FJC numbers show how New Jersey debtors use the bankruptcy remedy.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Can You Recover New Jersey Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

New Jersey Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Two-tier protection (N.J.S.A. 2A:17-56).

If you qualify, file the New Jersey exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in New Jersey

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a New Jersey creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

New Jersey exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See New Jersey bank account levy for the full playbook.

New Jersey Garnishment Duration and Release

In New Jersey, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most New Jersey judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - New Jersey judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, New Jersey law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

How to stop garnishment

Recover garnished wages

Emergency bankruptcy filing

Head-of-household exemption

New Jersey FDCPA and validation

New Jersey bankruptcy exemptions

New Jersey SSDI and garnishment

## Wage Garnishment in New York [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/new-york.html

Wage Garnishment in New York [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in New York

New York is one of the most debtor-friendly states for wage garnishment. The state-law cap is stricter than the federal 10% vs 25% CCPA floor, meaning creditors can take significantly less of your paycheck than in most states.

LimitRule

Maximum %10%

New York rule10% or CCPA minimum, whichever more protective.

Additional protectionVery strong protection (CPLR 5231); 30x federal MW floor.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Very strong protection (CPLR 5231); 30x federal MW floor.

## Wage Garnishment in North Carolina [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/north-carolina.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in North Carolina [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Carolina residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in North Carolina

North Carolina is one of four states (with Pennsylvania, North Carolina, and South Carolina) that generally bans wage garnishment for consumer debts. Your paycheck cannot be taken to pay credit card debt, medical bills, or most other unsecured consumer debts. Garnishment is only allowed for taxes, child support, student loans, and a few specific debt types.

LimitRule

Maximum %BANNED

North Carolina ruleWage garnishment generally NOT allowed for consumer debts (very strong protection).

Additional protectionAllowed only for taxes, student loans, and child support.

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

North Dakota exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See North Dakota bank account levy for the full playbook.

North Dakota Garnishment Duration and Release

In North Dakota, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most North Dakota judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - North Dakota judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, North Dakota law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

Related North Dakota Resources

How to stop garnishment

Recover garnished wages

Emergency bankruptcy filing

Head-of-household exemption

North Dakota FDCPA and validation

North Dakota bankruptcy exemptions

North Dakota SSDI and garnishment

## Wage Garnishment in Ohio [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/ohio.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Ohio [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Ohio

Ohio follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Ohio ruleFollows federal CCPA.

Additional protectionNo additional state limit beyond federal floor.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which Ohio Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In Ohio, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Ohio credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Ohio Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Ohio:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

When garnishment cannot be stopped administratively, bankruptcy's automatic stay halts it immediately. These FJC numbers show how Ohio debtors use the bankruptcy remedy.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 consumer bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Can You Recover Ohio Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Ohio Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

No additional state limit beyond federal floor.

If you qualify, file the Ohio exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Ohio

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Ohio creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Ohio exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Ohio bank account levy for the full playbook.

Ohio Garnishment Duration and Release

In Ohio, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Ohio judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Ohio judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Ohio law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

## Wage Garnishment in Pennsylvania [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/pennsylvania.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Pennsylvania [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Pennsylvania

Pennsylvania is one of four states (with Pennsylvania, North Carolina, and South Carolina) that generally bans wage garnishment for consumer debts. Your paycheck cannot be taken to pay credit card debt, medical bills, or most other unsecured consumer debts. Garnishment is only allowed for taxes, child support, student loans, and a few specific debt types.

LimitRule

Maximum %BANNED

Pennsylvania ruleWage garnishment generally NOT allowed for consumer debts (very strong protection).

Additional protectionAllowed only for taxes, child support, rent, student loans.

Your Rhode Island credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Rhode Island Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Rhode Island:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Can You Recover Rhode Island Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Rhode Island Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

No additional state limit.

If you qualify, file the Rhode Island exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Rhode Island

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Rhode Island creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Rhode Island exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Rhode Island bank account levy for the full playbook.

Rhode Island Garnishment Duration and Release

In Rhode Island, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Rhode Island judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Rhode Island judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Rhode Island law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

## Wage Garnishment in South Carolina [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/south-carolina.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in South Carolina [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Carolina residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in South Carolina

South Carolina is one of four states (with Pennsylvania, North Carolina, and South Carolina) that generally bans wage garnishment for consumer debts. Your paycheck cannot be taken to pay credit card debt, medical bills, or most other unsecured consumer debts. Garnishment is only allowed for taxes, child support, student loans, and a few specific debt types.

LimitRule

Maximum %BANNED

South Carolina ruleWage garnishment generally NOT allowed for consumer debts (very strong protection).

Additional protectionAllowed only for taxes, child support, and student loans.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which South Carolina Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In South Carolina, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your South Carolina credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop South Carolina Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in South Carolina:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

South Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

When garnishment cannot be stopped administratively, bankruptcy's automatic stay halts it immediately. These FJC numbers show how South Carolina debtors use the bankruptcy remedy.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 635 consumer bankruptcy cases from South Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

South Carolina Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Allowed only for taxes, child support, and student loans.

If you qualify, file the South Carolina exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in South Carolina

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a South Carolina creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

South Carolina exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See South Carolina bank account levy for the full playbook.

South Carolina Garnishment Duration and Release

In South Carolina, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most South Carolina judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - South Carolina judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, South Carolina law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

## Wage Garnishment in Utah [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/utah.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Utah [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Utah residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Utah

Utah follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Utah ruleFollows federal CCPA.

Additional protectionNo additional state limit.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which Utah Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In Utah, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Utah credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Utah Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Utah:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Can You Recover Utah Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Utah Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

No additional state limit.

If you qualify, file the Utah exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Utah

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Utah creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Utah exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Utah bank account levy for the full playbook.

Utah Garnishment Duration and Release

In Utah, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Utah judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Utah judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Utah law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

Related Utah Resources

Exempt income sources

How to stop garnishment

Recover garnished wages

Emergency bankruptcy filing

Head-of-household exemption

Utah FDCPA and validation

Utah bankruptcy exemptions

Utah SSDI and garnishment

## Wage Garnishment in Vermont [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/vermont.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Vermont [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Vermont residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Vermont

Vermont follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Vermont ruleFollows federal CCPA; lower-earner protections.

Additional protectionAdditional low-wage protection.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which Vermont Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In Vermont, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Vermont credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Vermont Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Vermont:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Can You Recover Vermont Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Vermont Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Additional low-wage protection.

If you qualify, file the Vermont exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Vermont

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Vermont creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Vermont exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Vermont bank account levy for the full playbook.

Vermont Garnishment Duration and Release

In Vermont, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Vermont judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Vermont judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Vermont law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Virginia residents.

Virginia follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Virginia ruleFollows federal CCPA; 40x federal minimum wage protected.

## Wage Garnishment in Washington [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/washington.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Washington [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Washington

Washington follows the federal CCPA wage-garnishment limit of 25% on disposable earnings, with a floor protecting at least 30 times the federal minimum wage.

LimitRule

Maximum %25%

Washington ruleFollows federal CCPA; 35x state minimum wage protected.

Additional protectionStronger than federal floor.

Washington Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Stronger than federal floor.

If you qualify, file the Washington exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Wage Garnishment Limits in West Virginia

West Virginia caps wage garnishment at 20% of disposable earnings, 5 percentage points better than the federal CCPA standard.

Maximum %20%

West Virginia rule20% max on disposable earnings (stricter than federal).

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - West Virginia judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, West Virginia law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.

## Wage Garnishment in Wisconsin [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It
Source: https://garnishedwages.org/states/wisconsin.html

← garnishedwages.org home

Wage Garnishment in Wisconsin [2026]: Limits, Exemptions, and How to Stop It

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wisconsin residents.

Wage Garnishment Limits in Wisconsin

Wisconsin caps wage garnishment at 20% of disposable earnings, 5 percentage points better than the federal CCPA standard.

LimitRule

Maximum %20%

Wisconsin rule20% max on disposable earnings (Wis. Stat. 812.34).

Additional protectionStrong worker protection.

Federal Floor (CCPA) - Applies in Every State

The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA) sets the national floor for wage garnishment protection. No state can go below it, but many states add stronger protection on top.

The CCPA formula: the garnishable amount is the LESSER of 25% of disposable earnings, OR the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr = $217.50/week).

"Disposable earnings" means gross pay minus legally required deductions (taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory retirement).

See exempt income sources for the full list of income streams that are completely off-limits to garnishment.

Which Wisconsin Debts Can Trigger Garnishment?

Not every debt creates garnishment rights. In Wisconsin, ordinary creditors must first:

File a lawsuit in state court and serve you with process.

Win a judgment - either by default (if you don't respond), summary judgment, or trial.

File a writ of garnishment with the court.

Serve the writ on your employer, who then begins withholding.

A few debts skip some of these steps:

Federal student loans - administrative wage garnishment up to 15% without a court order (ED-authorized).

IRS/state tax debts - administrative levy without court order.

Child support - automatic income withholding; generally 50-60% cap.

Court-ordered restitution - handled through court order directly.

Your Wisconsin credit card company cannot simply call your employer and start garnishment - they need the court process above. See our garnishment timeline guide.

How to Stop Wisconsin Garnishment Fast

Once garnishment begins, you have several options in Wisconsin:

Claim exemptions - head-of-household, low income, or specific income sources like SSDI/SSI. File the claim form promptly (deadlines are short).

Negotiate a settlement - some creditors will release the garnishment for a lump-sum payment at 40-60% of the debt.

File bankruptcy - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 freezes garnishment within 24 hours of filing. Wages already withheld but not yet remitted to the creditor may also be recoverable.

Motion to quash - if the underlying judgment was obtained in error (wrong defendant, improper service, SOL expired), you can move to vacate the judgment itself.

See the full stop-garnishment playbook and emergency bankruptcy filing.

Wisconsin Federal Bankruptcy Data

When garnishment cannot be stopped administratively, bankruptcy's automatic stay halts it immediately. These FJC numbers show how Wisconsin debtors use the bankruptcy remedy.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,541 consumer bankruptcy cases from Wisconsin's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 795399.4%0.4%

Chapter 1358848.1%51.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Can You Recover Wisconsin Wages Already Taken?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 547 (preference avoidance), wages garnished within 90 days before a bankruptcy filing can often be clawed back if the total garnished exceeds $600 and the debt was a pre-existing antecedent debt. The trustee recovers the money and returns it to the estate.

For consumer Chapter 7 filers, the practical test:

Was more than $600 garnished in the 90 days before filing?

Were you insolvent when the garnishment happened?

Is the creditor ordinary (not an insider)?

If yes to all three, file an objection or preference adversary. Details at getting money back after garnishment.

Wisconsin Head-of-Household and Low-Income Protection

Strong worker protection.

If you qualify, file the Wisconsin exemption claim immediately after garnishment begins. In most states, the deadline is within 10-20 days of the notice of garnishment.

Bank Account Levy in Wisconsin

A separate but related remedy is the bank account levy: instead of (or in addition to) wage garnishment, a Wisconsin creditor with a judgment can freeze your bank account and take funds directly. Key differences:

Single-strike hit. A levy takes everything in the account on the day of service (minus exempt amounts), not a percentage ongoing like wage garnishment.

Federal benefit protection. Treasury's 2011 rule protects the last two months of direct-deposited federal benefits (SSDI, SSI, VA, retirement) automatically.

Wisconsin exemption claim. You must file the exemption claim form promptly (often within 10-20 days) to preserve non-federal exempt amounts.

Commingling risk. If you deposit wages in the same account as federal benefits, the whole account can be frozen pending a hearing.

Keep federal benefits in a separate dedicated account when possible. See Wisconsin bank account levy for the full playbook.

Wisconsin Garnishment Duration and Release

In Wisconsin, a wage garnishment typically continues until one of the following:

Judgment is paid in full - principal, interest, and court costs. Most Wisconsin judgments accrue post-judgment interest at statutory rates.

Creditor voluntarily releases - usually after settlement negotiation for a lump-sum reduced amount.

Employment ends - garnishment does not automatically follow you to a new employer; the creditor must re-serve.

Bankruptcy filing - the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 halts garnishment immediately. Post-petition wages are part of your estate protections.

Successful exemption claim - head-of-household, low-income, or specific exempt-source findings.

Judgment expires - Wisconsin judgments have a limited lifespan (typically 10-20 years) unless renewed, though most creditors renew before expiration.

If multiple creditors have judgments, Wisconsin law generally applies a first-in-time rule: the first garnishment served runs until satisfied, then the next creditor in line takes priority.
